Strawman Structure of Network-Based Plan Identifier 
Every Car Has a VIN. Every Network Should Have a NIN. 
When you buy a car, it comes with a Vehicle Identification Number â€” a 17-character 
code stamped on the dashboard. That number tells any mechanic, dealer, insurer, or 
registry in the country exactly what the car is: who made it, what model it is, what 
engine is under the hood, and what year it was built. One number. Any system. Instant 
clarity. 
Health plan networks have no equivalent. A network has a name â€” but that name is a 
marketing label, not an identifier. It means something different in the directory, in the 
rate file, in the eligibility system, and on the claim. No two systems agree on what to call 
the same network, which means no two systems can reliably confirm they are talking 
about the same thing. 
The Network Identification Number fixes that. It is a structured identifier â€” nine 
positions, each one answering a specific question about the network â€” that travels 
consistently across every system that references networks: TiC files, provider 
directories, coverage records, digital insurance cards, and claims. 
The Problem 
Consumers pay for it â€” literally 
A member searches a directory, confirms their doctor is listed as in-network, books an 
appointment, and receives a surprise bill. Not because anyone acted in bad faith, but 
because the directory's definition of "in-network" does not match the claims system's 
definition â€” and there is no authoritative record that ties the two together. The No 
Surprises Act was designed to address exactly this outcome. Without a standard 
network identifier, enforcing it consistently is nearly impossible. 
Transparency mandates cannot deliver on their promise 
Congress and CMS have invested enormously in Transparency in Coverage rules 
requiring payers to publish machine-readable negotiated rate files. The intent was to 
enable consumers and developers to build reliable cost estimation tools. The reality is 
that TiC files are currently under federal review because they are too difficult to use. 
Rates are filed under plan names â€” marketing labels that change with product 
redesigns, are not consistent across payers, and do not map reliably to the provider 
panel a member actually has access to. A developer building a cost estimator must 
write custom logic for each payer just to determine which rates apply to which member. 
That is not transparency. That is complexity dressed up as disclosure. 
Multi-network complexity is invisible to everyone who needs to see it 
Most plans do not have one network â€” they have several. A commercial medical plan 
may have a primary care panel, a behavioral health carve-out managed by a separate 
organization, a pharmacy network managed by a PBM, a wrap network for out-of-area 
access, and tiered provider groupings within the primary panel. Each of these is a 
distinct network with distinct participation, distinct rates, and distinct rules. Today none 
of them have a stable shared identity that external systems can use. A provider's 
check-in system cannot tell which of these networks applies to a given member's 
behavioral health visit. A developer cannot build an app that routes a telehealth query to 
the right network. The complexity exists. The tools to navigate it do not. 
Why This Moment Is Different 
Three things are converging that make the network identity problem solvable â€” and 
urgent â€” right now. 
Federal scrutiny of TiC files is creating a forcing function. The current TiC 
machine-readable file structure is acknowledged to be broken. When CMS restructures 
the filing requirements, they will need a standard network identifier to anchor the new 
model. If payers do not bring a credible proposal to that process, the identifier will be 
defined without them â€” and without the operational nuance that reflects how networks 
actually work. 
FHIR infrastructure is now mature enough to support it. The payer-to-member and 
payer-to-provider FHIR APIs that went live under CMS interoperability rules provide the 
infrastructure on which a standard network identifier can travel consistently. The 
Coverage resource, InsurancePlan resource, ExplanationOfBenefit, and provider 
directory resources all have natural homes for a NIN. The pipes exist. They are just 
carrying inconsistent labels. 
Digital insurance cards are creating a natural integration point. As payers publish 
SMART Health Links and CARIN-compliant digital insurance cards, members will carry 
structured coverage data they can present at any care touchpoint. A NIN on that card is 
the missing link between "this member has coverage" and "this member is in-network 
for this service at this provider." Without it, the card is a display artifact. With it, the card 
is a machine-readable key. 
What We Are Proposing 
A Network Identification Number (NIN): a stable, structured identifier for a network 
instance built from nine elements of publicly available information. It is built on FHIR, 
uses existing resources where possible, and is designed to appear consistently across 
every transparency and interoperability artifact a payer produces. 
What the Schema Contains â€” And What It Deliberately Does Not 
The schema contains only what a consumer needs to make an informed coverage 
decision, what a developer needs to build a reliable tool, and what a regulator needs for 
TiC attribution. 
The following are outside this schema by design: how insurance risk is structured 
between the sponsor and the coverage program; how the network is reused or shared 
across the sponsor's product portfolio; which vendors or delegated entities manage or 
build the network; how providers within the network are paid; and which specific 
regulatory frameworks govern the network. These elements serve internal governance 
and contracting purposes. Their exposure would reveal commercially sensitive 
operational details that are not appropriate for public disclosure and are not required to 
answer any question a consumer, developer, or regulator legitimately needs answered. 
What's in a NIN? 
Each position answers one specific question. Together they give a complete, 
unambiguous description of the network. 
Segment 1 (S1) â€” What program governs this network? 
Every network exists within a statutory or market framework â€” Medicare Advantage, 
Medicaid managed care, commercial large group, standalone dental, and so on.  S1 
also carries population-type distinctions that affect consumer enrollment eligibility â€” 
D-SNP, C-SNP, I-SNP, PACE, and limited-benefit programs are expressed directly here 
so that one segment answers both "what program?" and "what population type?" 
Segment 2 (S2) â€” Who is responsible for this network? 
This is the issuer â€” the organization that built the network, maintains its accuracy, and 
is accountable for its TiC filing. The leading candidate is the Legal Entity Identifier (LEI) 
maintained by the GLEIF Global LEI Index â€” it is the only identifier that works for every 
sponsor type without special-casing, and the registry is free and publicly queryable.  
Segment 3 (S3) â€” Type of Plan? 
HMO. PPO. EPO. POS. This position answers the access question every member and 
provider needs answered before a visit 
Segment 4 (S4) â€” Is this network narrow, tiered, or broad? 
Not all PPOs are the same. So me have thousands of providers. Some have hundreds. 
Some split providers into preferred and standard tiers.  
Segment 5 (S5) â€” Is this the primary network or a specialized layer? 
Most members do not have one network â€” they have several. S5 says which one this 
NIN describes: primary, carve-out, tier, wrap, or contingency. This is what makes 
multi-network products computable.  
Segment 6 (S6) â€” Which benefits does this network cover? 
Medical. Behavioral health. Pharmacy. Dental. Vision. Dialysis. Home health. S6 lists 
the benefit types this network governs. It is repeating â€” one value per applicable 
domain. 
Segment 7 (S7) â€” Where does this network apply? 
S7 carries the computable geographic footprint of the network as a structured list of 
states, counties, or ZIP clusters. A provider's system checks S7 against a patient's 
home address or practice location before confirming participation. For networks with 
geographic gaps, excluded areas are enumerated explicitly â€” they are never implied.  
S8 â€” Which version of this network, and when is it effective? 
Networks change. Providers join and leave. Geographic scope expands and contracts. 
S8 timestamps the network configuration. Every NIN carries an effective date and an 
end date.  
S9 â€” Who can access this network? 
Some networks are open to any eligible member. Some are restricted to employees of a 
specific employer. Some require a clinical diagnosis for access. S9 states the constraint 
clearly â€” so a shopping tool does not show a consumer a network they cannot actually 
enroll in, and a provider does not check in a patient under coverage they are not eligible 
for. S9 answers "can I get this?" without revealing the commercial arrangement behind 
the restriction. 
What a NIN Looks Like in Practice 
A large regional carrier offers a standard PPO for commercial group clients across four 
Mid-Atlantic states. Their NIN reads: 
Position 
What It Says 
S1 â€” Program type 
Commercial Large Group 
S2 â€” Sponsor 
{Carrier identifier (LEI?)} 
S3 â€” Network design 
PPO 
S4 â€” Breadth modifier 
Standard 
S5 â€” Role 
Primary 
S6 â€” Service scope 
Medical/Surgical, Behavioral Health 
S7 â€” Geographic scope 
PA, NJ, DE, MD 
S8 â€” Version 
2027 Plan Year â€” Jan 1 to Dec 31, 2027 
S9 â€” Eligibility constraint 
None 
That NIN is available through SMART Health Links, CARIN Blue Button, and published 
What This Fixes 
For members: Your directory search, your cost estimate, and your claim are all looking 
at the same network. If your doctor shows as in-network, they get billed as in-network. 
For providers: One query to verify participation. One query to look up the rate. No phone 
calls. No eligibility guessing. No retroactive disputes because the network definition 
changed between the visit and the adjudication. 
For developers: Building a cost estimator no longer requires custom integration for 
every payer. The NIN is the same identifier in the rate file and on the card. Rate lookup 
is a clean three-key query: network, provider, service code. 
For regulators: TiC files, directory accuracy complaints, and network adequacy filings all 
reference the same network identifier. The restructured TiC filing model that CMS is 
working toward has a natural anchor. 
FHIR Implementation 
The NIN lives in the FHIR InsurancePlan resource. Where existing FHIR fields support 
a segment natively, those fields are used. Where they do not, a standard extension 
carries the segment. Every segment uses a consistent pattern that always carries a 
segment code and a value together â€” never one without the other. The NIN propagates 
across four FHIR surfaces: InsurancePlan (authoritative record), Coverage (member's 
card), ExplanationOfBenefit (claims record), and PractitionerRole / 
OrganizationAffiliation (directory participation with effective dates). Full 
implementation specifications are in Appendix B. 
How Payers Tie Providers to a NIN 
The NIN does not replace a payer's existing provider data management systems. It 
gives those systems a stable external key to publish against. 
The payer workflow to implement NINs has three steps: 
Step 1 â€” Assign NINs to networks. Once per network configuration, per plan year. A 
payer with twelve distinct network configurations issues twelve NINs. This is a data 
governance exercise, not an ongoing operational burden. 
Step 2 â€” Map internal panel records to NINs. Every provider contract row in the PDM 
that today says "Commercial PPO Panel" or "IL-BH-CARVEOUT" gets tagged with the 
corresponding NIN. This is the one-time translation work. Once the mapping exists it 
carries forward to each plan year's version NIN automatically. 
Step 3 â€” Publish the mapping. The payer's FHIR directory publishes the participation 
as PractitionerRole records (for individual providers) and OrganizationAffiliation 
records (for facilities and groups). Each record carries: 
â—â€‹ The provider or facility identifier (NPI) 
â—â€‹ A reference to the InsurancePlan carrying the NIN 
â—â€‹ The contract effective and end dates 
â—â€‹ The practice location(s) covered 
â—â€‹ The specialty and service types covered under this participation 
When a provider leaves a network, their participation record is retired with an end date 
â€” never deleted. When a new version NIN is issued for plan year renewal, new 
participation records are published referencing the new NIN. The prior year's records 
remain queryable for dispute resolution and audit. 
Enabling Unambiguous Queries Regarding Individual NPI Participation 
 
Another significant benefit of a NIN is enabling definitive Yes/No queries about a 
providerâ€™s participation in a network. Currently queries about network participation can 
only return results that the client has to match against a reference set of information 
about plans. However, because of the structure of a NIN, the network can be referenced 
as a well-defined entity and validated against known networks from the payer. 
Because the NIN is the authoritative identifier of the network, a query can formed that 
allows an unambiguous answer. An application can send a NIN and an NPI 
GET 
/PractitionerRole?practitioner.identifier=NPI|1234567890&OrganizationalAffiliation=NIN|
98765 
And get back a set of status codes: 
â€œIn-Networkâ€ 
â€œOut-of-Networkâ€ 
â€œOther-Relationshipâ€ 
 
How Providers Know Which Networks They Participate In 
This is one of the most broken parts of the current system â€” and it is broken 
independent of the NIN. 
Today a provider learns about their network participation through participation letters at 
contract execution, remittance advice after claims pay at unexpected rates, 
payer-specific web portals that require separate logins for every payer relationship, and 
credentialing databases that track credentialing status but not participation by specific 
network configuration. None of these give a provider a machine-readable, current, 
auditable list of which network configurations they are in across all their payer 
relationships. 
The NIN changes this in two ways. 
Payer-side directory lookup. When payers publish NIN-keyed PractitionerRole and 
OrganizationAffiliation records in their FHIR directories, those directories become 
queryable by NPI. A provider â€” or their EHR or practice management system â€” queries 
any payer's directory: 
GET /PractitionerRole?practitioner.identifier=NPI|1234567890 
And gets back every NIN that provider participates in at that payer, described in 
consistent terms, with effective and end dates. Because NINs use a standard schema 
across payers, the response is interpretable without custom integration. 
Cross-payer aggregation. Because every payer's NIN-keyed directory uses the same 
schema, a neutral party â€” a clearinghouse, a credentialing organization, or a payer 
consortium â€” can aggregate participation records across payers into a single 
provider-facing view. A provider looks up their NPI and sees every network they 
participate in, across all payer relationships, described in consistent terms. That does 
not exist today because there is no common network identifier. The NIN makes it 
structurally possible for the first time. 
The Notification Gap 
The NIN also creates a foundation for proactive provider notification â€” something that 
does not exist today at all. 
When a payer issues a new version NIN or retires an existing one, affected providers 
should know. Today that notification is a participation letter â€” a PDF that may or may 
not be read, filed, or acted on. With NIN-keyed FHIR directories, a provider's practice 
management system can subscribe to changes in the participation records that 
reference their NPI: 
"Notify me when any PractitionerRole referencing NPI 1234567890 and 
NIN-2027-ABC123 changes." 
FHIR Subscription resources support exactly this pattern. When a payer retires a NIN, 
terminates a provider's participation, or issues a new plan-year version, the subscribing 
system receives a notification automatically. The provider does not discover the change 
on a remittance advice thirty days after the fact. 
What This Proposal Does Not Solve 
The NIN is a necessary condition for all of this to work. It is not a sufficient condition. 
The sufficient condition is payer commitment to accurate, timely, NIN-keyed FHIR 
directory publication. Directory accuracy is already a regulatory obligation under existing 
CMS and state rules. The NIN does not add to that obligation â€” it gives it a structure 
that makes compliance verifiable and provider-facing lookup tractable. But a NIN 
published against an inaccurate provider roster is still an inaccurate directory. The NIN 
surfaces the problem more clearly. It does not eliminate the need for the operational 
discipline to fix it. 
Appendix A: NIN Public Schema with Representative Values 
This appendix defines the eleven elements of the public NIN schema. Representative 
values are shown inline for each element. These are illustrative â€” they show the 
structure and vocabulary without claiming to be exhaustive. Full value sets will be

analysis:
# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Not provided; commenter proposes a Network Identification Number (NIN) framework.
- **Stakeholder type:** Individual / Other (standards proposal; likely health IT/interoperability stakeholder)
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** No formal credentials stated. The comment demonstrates familiarity with FHIR, Transparency in Coverage files, SMART Health Links, CARIN Blue Button, provider directories, claims, and payer network operations.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

The commenter proposes creation of a structured Network Identification Number (NIN) to give health plan networks a stable, computable identity across Transparency in Coverage files, provider directories, digital insurance cards, coverage records, and claims. The comment is broadly supportive of FHIR-based interoperability infrastructure but asks CMS to address a gap not directly covered by the proposed drug prior authorization rule: consistent identification of payer networks for transparency, in-network status, cost estimation, and directory accuracy.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING; ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE; GENERAL.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** No CFR citations mentioned. The comment refers generally to Transparency in Coverage requirements and the No Surprises Act.
- **Standards referenced:** FHIR; FHIR InsurancePlan, Coverage, ExplanationOfBenefit, PractitionerRole, OrganizationAffiliation, Location, and Subscription resources; SMART Health Links; CARIN Blue Button; Legal Entity Identifier (LEI) and GLEIF Global LEI Index.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Standard Network Identification Number**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** The commenter argues that plan network names are marketing labels that do not map consistently across directories, rate files, eligibility systems, claims, and digital insurance cards. This inconsistency undermines consumer cost estimation, directory accuracy, surprise billing protections, and regulatory oversight.
- **Specific request:** CMS should adopt or facilitate development of a structured NIN schema that uniquely identifies network instances using standardized, public elements.

**Topic 2: FHIR Implementation of Network Identity**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Clarify / Modify
- **Rationale:** The commenter states that existing FHIR infrastructure is mature enough to carry NINs and that the InsurancePlan resource can serve as the authoritative record, with NINs propagated through Coverage, ExplanationOfBenefit, PractitionerRole, and OrganizationAffiliation resources.
- **Specific request:** CMS should recognize a standard FHIR implementation pattern for NINs, using native FHIR fields where available and standard extensions where necessary.

**Topic 3: Transparency in Coverage and Directory Accuracy**
- **Provision ID:** API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** The commenter argues that current TiC files cannot reliably support consumer tools because rates are associated with inconsistent plan or network labels. A NIN would allow public endpoints, directories, and rate files to reference the same network.
- **Specific request:** CMS should use a standard network identifier as an anchor when restructuring TiC machine-readable files and related public API artifacts.

**Topic 4: Provider Participation Query and Notification**
- **Provision ID:** ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE
- **Position:** Clarify
- **Rationale:** The commenter describes how NIN-keyed FHIR directory records could support yes/no queries about provider participation and enable FHIR Subscription-based notifications when network participation changes.
- **Specific request:** CMS and ONC should support standard resource usage and vocabulary needed for NIN-keyed provider directory lookup and network participation change notifications.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S1:** The comment indirectly supports requiring implementation guidance when needed for consistent interoperability, arguing that inconsistent labels prevent systems from reliably identifying the same network.
- **S6:** The comment references CARIN Blue Button and digital insurance cards, recommending that network identifiers travel with member coverage data.
- **S8:** The comment references SMART Health Links as a natural integration point for carrying structured coverage and network data on digital insurance cards.
- **S9:** The comment discusses FHIR Subscriptions as a mechanism for notifying providers when NIN-keyed participation records change.
- **S23:** The comment indirectly addresses public API endpoint usefulness, recommending that payer-published artifacts include a stable network identifier while excluding commercially sensitive internal contracting information.
- **S24:** The comment suggests specific technical details that should be represented consistently across public artifacts, including network sponsor, plan design, breadth, role, service scope, geography, version dates, and eligibility constraints.
- **S60:** The comment proposes a standards-based approach using existing FHIR resources and extensions, relevant to ONC versioning and standards adoption discussions.
- **S66-S82:** The comment is best treated as a general interoperability RFI response proposing a new network identity layer for transparency, directories, digital cards, claims, and notifications.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Establish a Network Identification Number as a stable, structured identifier for health plan network instances.
2. Build the NIN schema from public, consumer- and regulator-relevant elements rather than internal contracting or risk-sharing details.
3. Represent the NIN in FHIR InsurancePlan as the authoritative network record and propagate it through Coverage, ExplanationOfBenefit, PractitionerRole, and OrganizationAffiliation resources.
4. Require or encourage payers to map internal provider panel records to NINs and publish NIN-keyed provider participation records with effective and end dates.
5. Use NINs to anchor restructured Transparency in Coverage files, provider directory accuracy monitoring, digital insurance cards, and network adequacy oversight.
6. Support NIN-based yes/no provider participation queries and FHIR Subscription notifications for network changes.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Existing network names are inconsistent across payer systems and public artifacts; TiC files are hard to use; multi-network plan designs are not computable; provider participation status cannot be queried reliably.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Consumers may rely on directories that do not match claims adjudication and receive surprise bills; developers must create payer-specific logic; providers discover network changes through delayed claims or portal lookups; regulators cannot easily connect rate files, directories, complaints, and adequacy filings.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Payers must map internal panel records to NINs, publish accurate NIN-keyed FHIR directories, retain version history, and maintain timely participation data.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Consumers, providers, payers, developers, regulators, clearinghouses, credentialing organizations, PBMs, and organizations responsible for digital insurance cards and provider directories.

- **Technical feasibility:** The comment states that FHIR infrastructure is mature enough and identifies specific FHIR resources suitable for implementation, but acknowledges that directory accuracy and payer operational discipline remain necessary.
- **Patient care impact:** The proposal could improve patient access and financial predictability by making in-network status and cost estimates more reliable before care is delivered.
